<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a well-established risk factor for adverse cardiovascular outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). However, research assessing the magnitude and the timing of clinical events over the long term in patients with DM undergoing PCI with a drug-eluting stent (DES) is limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The data of patients treated with DES in five randomized controlled trials with available 10-year follow-up were pooled. Patients were grouped according their DM diagnosis at baseline. The primary endpoint was all-cause death. The secondary endpoints were cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction (MI), definite stent thrombosis (ST), target lesion revascularization (TLR), target vessel revascularization (TVR) and non-target vessel revascularization (nTVR). All-cause death was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, whereas cumulative incidence functions accounting for the competing risk of death were calculated for secondary endpoints. Associations were evaluated using both cause-specific Cox regression, yielding cause-specific hazard ratios (HRs), and Fine-Gray regression, yielding subdistribution hazard ratios (sHRs). Multivariable analyses with adjustment for relevant variables and subgroup analyses were performed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Among 9,699 patients, 2,298 had DM at baseline. Compared with patients without DM, patients with DM had a higher risk of all-cause death (adjusted hazard ratio [HR
                      <jats:sub>adj</jats:sub>
                      ] 1.68 [95% confidence interval 1.59–1.78]) and cardiovascular death (HR
                      <jats:sub>adj</jats:sub>
                      1.74 [1.63–1.87]) up to 10 years. The risks of definite ST (HR
                      <jats:sub>adj</jats:sub>
                      1.55 [1.18–2.04]), TLR (HR
                      <jats:sub>adj</jats:sub>
                      1.35 [1.21–1.51]), TVR (HR
                      <jats:sub>adj</jats:sub>
                      1.28 [1.14–1.43]), and nTVR (HR
                      <jats:sub>adj</jats:sub>
                      1.23 [1.09–1.40]) were significantly increased in patients with DM. Landmark analyses showed endpoint-specific temporal patterns: the excess MI risk was predominantly observed within the first month, whereas the excess definite ST risk was detected between 30 days and 1 year. Notably, the association between DM at baseline and clinical outcomes varied across subgroups defined by age, sex, clinical presentation, and DES-generation (all P
                      <jats:sub>interaction</jats:sub>
                      <0.001). Insulin-treated patients represent the higher risk phenotype.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DM was associated with distinct temporal patterns of adverse outcomes after PCI with DES, with an early associations with MI and definite ST, as well as an increased risk of death and repeat revascularisation in the longer term. These findings further emphasize the need for intensified secondary prevention and provide a long-term benchmark against which novel management strategies should be evaluated in patients with DM undergoing PCI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Diabetes mellitus and 10-year clinical outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents: insights from the DECADE cooperation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Apolipoprotein CIII (apoCIII) is a key regulator of triglyceride metabolism and an emerging biomarker of cardiometabolic risk. Although elevated total apoCIII concentrations have been associated with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and cardiovascular disease, individual apoCIII proteoforms may exert distinct metabolic effects. We investigated the prospective associations between apoCIII proteoforms and incident T2D in adults at high cardiometabolic risk, as well as their associations with dietary intake.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This nested case-control study included 594 incident T2D cases and 594 controls matched for age, sex, intervention group, body mass index, fasting glucose and triglyceride concentrations. Seven apoCIII proteoforms were measured using mass spectrometry-based immunoassay, and total apoCIII concentrations were measured using an immunoturbidimetric assay. Associations between apoCIII proteoforms and metabolic traits, dietary factors, and incident T2D were evaluated using multivariable-adjusted regression models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ApoCIII proteoforms showed heterogeneous associations with metabolic risk and incident T2D. Higher CIII2d/CIII1, CIII2/CIII1, and CIII0f/CIII1 ratios were associated with more favourable lipid and glycaemic profiles and lower odds of incident T2D per 1-SD increase (CIII2d/CIII1 OR = 0.77, 95% CI: 0.61–0.97; CIII2/CIII1 OR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.69–0.96; CIII0f/CIII1 OR = 0.73, 95% CI: 0.55–0.97). Exploratory analyses identified several nominal associations between dietary intake and apoCIII proteoform ratios; however, none remained statistically significant after FDR correction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher CIII2d/CIII1, CIII2/CIII1, and CIII0f/CIII1 proteoform ratios were associated with healthier lipid and glucose metabolic profiles and lower odds of incident T2D. These findings support further investigation of apoCIII proteoform profiling as a potential biomarker of incident T2D risk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Specific apoCIII proteoform ratios are associated with a healthier cardiometabolic phenotype and lower incidence of type 2 diabetes: a nested case-control study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A patient-linked in-vitro model system to investigate the interplay of cardiac and vascular cells offers opportunities to understand pathogenesis. Here we establish that novel 3D structure of iPSC-derived vascularised cardiac organoids (VCO), originated from donors with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) demonstrate pronounced mechanistic, cellular and mitochondrial dysfunction when compared to non-diabetic counterparts. Integrated RNA sequencing, functional assays, and RT-PCR analyses identified novel molecular signatures indicative of mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy. Notably, these analyses demonstrated a significant upregulation of TINF2, a telomeric protein and key components of the shelterin complex. To our knowledge, the involvement of TINF2 has not previously been reported in cardiac or vascular-specific cell types, nor altered in T2DM. Transgenic targeting of TINF2 was associated with reversing of the targets of T2DM-related mitochondrial dysfunction and was associated with restoring of mitophagy. Our findings reveal the potentially vital role of the TINF2 protein in T2DM-associated mitochondrial dysfunction and the potential for re-targeting mitophagy for the treatment of T2DM.</jats:p>
title: Increased expression of TINF2 is associated with impaired cardiac mitophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction in type 2 diabetes revealed by donor-derived vascularised cardiac organoids
